config.title: fs module mastery

intro.title: fs module mastery
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple file system explorer that reads and displays the contents of a directory using Node.js. You will learn the core programming concept of file system operations, focusing on asynchronous methods to handle I/O without blocking your program. The main technologies involved are the built-in Node.js 'fs' module and JavaScript's async/await syntax for managing asynchronous code. By the end, you'll be able to list files, read their details, and handle errors gracefully in a beginner-friendly way.
intro.usecase: The fs module is foundational for any Node.js application that interacts with the file system. In real-world software, this pattern appears in content management systems where administrators upload and organize files, in build tools that process project assets, and in data processing pipelines that read and transform large datasets. Developers use fs operations to implement features like user profile picture uploads, log file analysis for debugging, and configuration file management for application settings. Mastering these file operations is essential for building robust backend services, automation scripts, and data-driven applications.

objectives: Implement file reading operations using fs.readFile and fs.readFileSync
Construct file writing operations with fs.writeFile and fs.writeFileSync
Manipulate file metadata using fs.stat and fs.access methods
Apply directory operations including creation, listing, and removal
Integrate error handling patterns for file system operations
Configure file streams for reading and writing large files
Control file permissions and ownership through fs.chmod and fs.chown

steps.title: Import the fs module
steps.instruction: Import the fs module using require() and assign it to a constant named fs.
steps.hint: Use the require() function with the string 'fs' to import the module.
steps.analogousExample:
// Importing another core module
const path = require('path');
steps.expectedOutcome: The fs module is imported and ready to use for file system operations.
successCriteria: The fs module is imported using require() and assigned to a constant named fs.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're using require('fs') and assigning it to a constant named fs.
steps.feedbackWrong: The fs module needs to be imported using require('fs') and assigned to a constant named fs.

steps.title: Create a main function to demonstrate fs operations
steps.instruction: Create an async function named main that will contain all the file system operations. The function should be empty for now.
steps.hint: Use the async keyword before function to make it asynchronous. Name it exactly 'main'.
steps.seedCode:
const fs = require('fs');

// Create your async main function here
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have an empty async main function ready to hold file system operations.
successCriteria: An async function named main is defined.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure the function is named 'main' and uses the async keyword.
steps.feedbackWrong: The function isn't defined correctly. Check that it's named 'main' and marked as async.

steps.title: Initialize test file path and content variables
steps.instruction: Inside your main function, create two variables: one named 'filePath' with the value './test.txt', and another named 'fileContent' with the value 'Hello from fs module!'.
steps.hint: Use the 'const' keyword to declare variables inside your function. The file path should be a string, and the content should also be a string.
steps.expectedOutcome: Your main function will have two variables ready to use in file operations.
successCriteria: The main function contains 'filePath' and 'fileContent' variables with the specified string values.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You created some variables, but make sure you have both 'filePath' and 'fileContent' with the exact values specified.
steps.feedbackWrong: The variables weren't created correctly. Check that you have both 'filePath' and 'fileContent' inside the main function.

steps.title: Write a file using fs.writeFile
steps.instruction: Inside your main function, use fs.writeFile to create a new file with the test content you initialized earlier.
steps.hint: Call fs.writeFile with the file path, content, and a callback function that handles errors.
steps.expectedOutcome: The main function now contains a call to fs.writeFile that will create a file with your test content.
successCriteria: fs.writeFile is called with the correct arguments: file path, content, and a callback function.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using fs.writeFile with all required arguments.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check the syntax: fs.writeFile needs the file path, content, and a callback function.

steps.title: Read a file using fs.readFile
steps.instruction: Inside your main function, add code to read the file you just created using fs.readFile. Use the same filePath variable and log the file content to the console.
steps.hint: Remember that fs.readFile is asynchronous. Use await with fs.readFile to get the file content, then console.log to display it.
steps.expectedOutcome: The code will read the file created in the previous step and log its content to the console.
successCriteria: The main function includes an await fs.readFile call with the filePath variable and logs the result using console.log.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using await with fs.readFile and logging the result with console.log. Check that you're using the same filePath variable.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's focus on adding the fs.readFile call inside the main function. Use await fs.readFile(filePath, 'utf8') to read the file, then console.log to display the content.

steps.title: Append to a file using fs.appendFile
steps.instruction: Inside your main function, after the readFile operation, use fs.appendFile to add more content to the existing test.txt file.
steps.hint: Call fs.appendFile with the file path and the new content you want to add. Remember to use await since it returns a promise.
steps.analogousExample:
// Appending content to a file
await fs.appendFile('./log.txt', 'New log entry\n');
steps.expectedOutcome: The main function now includes an fs.appendFile call to modify the existing file by adding more content.
successCriteria: fs.appendFile is called with the correct file path and additional content string inside the main function.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure fs.appendFile is called with the file path and the content to append.
steps.feedbackWrong: The fs.appendFile operation is missing or incorrect. Check that you're calling fs.appendFile with the file path and content inside the main function.

steps.title: Check if file exists using fs.existsSync
steps.instruction: Inside your main function, after the append operation, use fs.existsSync to check if the file exists and log the result.
steps.hint: Call fs.existsSync with the filePath variable, then log the boolean result with console.log.
steps.expectedOutcome: The learner adds synchronous file existence checking to verify the file is present after previous operations.
successCriteria: The code includes fs.existsSync(filePath) and logs the result with console.log.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using fs.existsSync with the filePath variable and logging the result.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's focus on this step: use fs.existsSync to check if the file exists and log the boolean result.

steps.title: Get file information using fs.stat
steps.instruction: Inside the main function, after the file existence check, use fs.stat to get information about the file (size, creation time, etc.) and log the stats object.
steps.hint: Use await fs.stat(filePath) to get the file stats, then console.log the stats object to see all the metadata.
steps.expectedOutcome: The code will retrieve and display file metadata including size, creation time, and modification time.
successCriteria: fs.stat is called with the filePath, and the stats object is logged to the console.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you're using fs.stat with the filePath and logging the result. Check that you're using await since fs.stat returns a promise.
steps.feedbackWrong: use fs.stat to get file information. Remember to use the filePath variable and log the stats object.

steps.title: Delete a file using fs.unlink
steps.instruction: Inside your main function, after the fs.stat operation, use fs.unlink to delete the test file.
steps.hint: Remember that fs.unlink is asynchronous and returns a promise. Use await with it and pass the filePath variable as the argument.
steps.analogousExample:
// Similar: deleting a file
await fs.unlink('./file-to-delete.txt');
steps.expectedOutcome: The test.txt file will be deleted from the filesystem when the main function runs.
successCriteria: fs.unlink is called with the filePath variable inside the main function.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're calling fs.unlink with the correct file path variable.
steps.feedbackWrong: The file deletion step is missing. Remember to use fs.unlink with the filePath variable.

steps.title: Call the main function and handle errors
steps.instruction: Call the main function at the bottom of your file and wrap it in a try/catch block to handle any errors.
steps.hint: Use try { await main(); } catch (error) { console.error('Error:', error); } to execute and catch errors.
steps.expectedOutcome: The main function is executed and any errors are caught and logged to the console.
successCriteria: main is called inside a try/catch block that logs errors to the console.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're calling main() inside a try/catch block and logging any errors.
steps.feedbackWrong: The main function isn't being called with error handling. Add a try/catch block that calls main() and logs errors.
